brief.topic: Six People Force a Pattern You Cannot Avoid

creative.audience: Curious teens and adults; concrete visual reasoning before specialist terminology.
creative.learning_goal: Prove the six-person friends-or-strangers theorem and show five is insufficient.
creative.question: Can we avoid both groups?
creative.payoff: Five admits a counterexample; crossings are not vertices.
creative.duration_rationale: Four causal sequences with a prediction, mechanism, explanation and changed case; measured narration determines duration.

scenes.narration: Put six people in a room. For every pair, either they know each other or they do not. Assume knowing is mutual. No matter how you arrange those relationships, three people must all know each other, or three must all be strangers to one another. Can you connect the room without creating either group? Draw a solid teal line for acquaintances, and a dashed red line for strangers. The unavoidable group becomes a triangle with three matching edges.

Pick one person, A. There are five connections leaving A. At least three have the same type, because two of each would only account for four. Suppose A knows B, C, and D. Now forget everyone else and inspect the three connections among those people. If B and C know each other, we already have a triangle of acquaintances: A knows B, A knows C, and B knows C. One matching edge among the neighbors is enough.

What if none of those three pairs know each other? Then B, C, and D are three mutual strangers. Either way, the required group exists. And if A originally had three stranger connections instead, swap the roles of acquaintances and strangers in the same argument. Every possible room is covered by these cases. We did not inspect every network. We found a small pattern that every six-person network is forced to contain.

Could five people be enough? Arrange five dots in a circle. Make neighboring pairs acquaintances, and all diagonal pairs strangers. The solid edges form a pentagon, so they contain no triangle. The dashed diagonals form a five-pointed star, also with no triangle among the five people. Crossings are not extra people. So five can avoid the pattern, while six cannot. This is a first glimpse of Ramsey theory: enough relationships can force order, even when you try to avoid it.
